chunks: What is a wafer?. The question: What is a wafer?
A wafer is a thin, round disc of extremely pure silicon on which chips are built.
The silicon is a single crystal, which means its atoms form one continuous, orderly pattern, so every transistor behaves the same.
Hundreds or thousands of identical chips are built on one wafer at once, then cut apart. Making many chips together makes each one cheaper.
Think of a round tray of muffin cups. You bake every muffin in one oven run, so the oven cost is shared across all of them.
A bigger tray holds more muffins for nearly the same oven run, so each muffin costs less. A wafer is the tray and each chip site is a muffin cup.
Cups at the curved edge do not fit a whole square, so some area is wasted.
Dies per wafer fall roughly as 1/area. At 100 mm² a 300 mm wafer holds about 640 candidate dies versus 270 on 200 mm.
For big dies the edge loss term matters more, which is another cost penalty for large chips ("Why chips can't be arbitrarily large").
Single-crystal silicon: silicon whose atoms form one unbroken, orderly pattern. Ingot: the long crystal cylinder that wafers are sliced from.
Die: one rectangular chip site on the wafer. Scribe lane: the thin strip between dies where the wafer is later sawn apart.
Notch: a small cut in the wafer's edge that marks the crystal direction.
A 300 mm wafer has an area of π times 150² about 70,700 mm². For dies of 100 mm² each, dividing gives about 707.
The dies at the curved edge are partial, so only about 640 whole dies fit. A 200 mm wafer, with an area of about 31,400 mm², fits about 270. The 300 mm wafer has 2.
25 times the area but about 2. 4 times the dies, so it is cheaper per die. Yield, the share of dies that work, is a separate question. See "Chip fabrication yield considerations".
That is the whole idea.
"A wafer is a thin, polished disc of ultra-pure single-crystal silicon, usually 300 mm across and about 0.
775 mm thick, on which hundreds or thousands of identical chips are built at the same time. It's grown as a crystal ingot by the Czochralski method, sliced and polished.
Dies are cut from it later. Bigger wafers mean more dies per processing step, which lowers cost per chip."
